cells.tense: Here with the pen: the practice is running and the hoping is being kept, one repeat at a time.
cells.ask: Show one person the dullest part of your practice — the repeats nobody watches — and let them see what it holds.
cells.core: You sit down to the same small work and it answers back. Not dramatic, not loud — the plain repetitions done again this week because they were done last week. Plenty of people want a sign before they keep going. You already have the thing itself, earned in private where nobody claps, and the hoping sits on top of it instead of the other way around.\n\nSo the practice carries the hope, not the hope carrying the practice. You're not producing proof for anyone and not waiting on a mood. Hands on the work, the same corner, the same hour — and when the sky stays blank, there's still something solid under you. Keep that going, and show it to someone once.
cells.sheetLine: The repeats are real, and the hope rides on them.
cells.verb: keeping a steady small practice alight
cells.place: a corner kept for repeating the same small work by hand

cells.tense: Bracing at a future you can't write in: the practice has become a machine against bad days that haven't arrived.
cells.ask: Skip one repetition this week and leave the questions that come up unanswered for a day.
cells.core: The work gets done, the finished thing shines a little, and the hoping holds without strain — that is the whole of it, and it doesn't ask much of you. What you're doing instead is rehearsal. Every repetition gets asked to prove it can survive something: a bad month, a bad year. The proving has moved into the work itself, and the time to actually do it keeps getting spent on preparing to keep doing it.\n\nWhat gets lost is what the work was for: the quiet shine of something made with your hands. You keep talking over the part of you that already weighs things and lands on an answer. Let the questions stay open for one day, and hear that before you argue with it.
cells.sheetLine: You're rehearsing the work against a hard day that hasn't come.

cells.tense: Still standing at a door that's behind you: the discipline once kept has thinned to almost nothing.
cells.ask: Pick the smallest piece of the old practice — five minutes, done badly — and restart it three times this week.
cells.core: Kept well, this is a small light tended by attention, and the hope rides on it without being pushed. There's a shelf where the practice used to live and you walk past it. You kept a small discipline going once and it held you; somewhere in there the repeats stopped, and being careful with yourself looked like not making a big deal of it. Care now has to arrive quietly, done by hand before it feels like anything.\n\nThat's the way back, not a bigger push. Your light doesn't need relighting by force or by a lecture — only tending. Start it small, keep turning up, and the hope you carry will have somewhere to stand while it waits.
cells.sheetLine: The practice thinned out. It starts again small.
cells.verb: keeping a steady small practice alight

cells.tense: Pen down in a room you're already writing: the practice is holding you and you haven't claimed it.
cells.ask: Name one thing your repeated work has carried you through, and say out loud that it was yours.
cells.core: This is already running. You keep something lit through hard patches — the same repeated work, the same quiet returns — and the hoping gets carried by that, not by luck and not by circumstance. Ask how you got through and you say you just did, which skips the part where you built the thing one rep at a time and kept showing up on the days it felt like nothing.\n\nNo speech needed. The work is yours already; the saying so is what hasn't happened. Name one thing it carried you through, out loud, and let the claim catch up with what your hands have been doing.
cells.sheetLine: You've kept it lit and called it just getting through.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that steady repetition is what keeps this hope alive; the record also says persistence here is a form of faith and can exist mostly in argument with oneself. A reader could reasonably say they have never had a practice to abandon, so the Too Little ask should stand as an offer rather than a diagnosis. The asks survive a wrong read because each one is small, private, and useful to anyone, careful or coasting. The sentence that serves me more than them is 'the work kept you hoping' — it sounds like a verdict, so the cells keep the work as something they do, not something owed.
